title: Remembering, I live
hookLine: aakhaa jeevaa visrai mar jaao: chanting I live, forgetting I die (Asa, ang 9)

cards: A busy day. Meetings back to back, errands, messages. Somewhere around noon you meant to eat and didn't.
By four o'clock you're snapping at people, the screen is blurry, everything feels harder than it should. And then it hits you: I forgot lunch. You weren't failing at life.
You'd just forgotten the thing that keeps you going, and the cost showed up everywhere else. Tonight's shabad reaches for hunger too.

teach.h: AAKHAA JEEVAA: SAYING IT, I LIVE.
teach.b: The third shabad of Rehras, Guru Nanak in Raag Asa, opens with this line: aakhaa jeevaa visrai mar jaao. Saying it, I live; forgetting, I die. It, here, is the Name.
Then, straight away, honesty: it's hard to say the True Name. Not hard to pronounce.

teach.h: IT'S HARD TO KEEP SAYING THE NAME.
teach.b: Hard to keep saying, to keep remembering, through a day full of everything else. And then the hunger picture.

teach.h: HUNGER FOR THE NAME EATS PAIN.
teach.b: If a person feels hunger for the True Name, the shabad says in paraphrase, that hunger eats up their pain. That's a reversal. Usually hunger is the problem.
Here, the right hunger is the cure: wanting the Name so much that the wanting itself consumes sorrow. The refrain asks: so kio visrai meree maae.

teach.h: HOW COULD I FORGET, MY MOTHER?
teach.b: How could I forget Him, my mother? You've heard that address before: meree maae, my mother, is how the Anand began. Here it's a plea, almost a worry: how could I ever forget?
The shabad goes on to say that even if everyone gathered to praise Him, He wouldn't grow greater, and if no one did, He wouldn't grow less.
He doesn't die, and there's no mourning for Him; He keeps on giving, and His gifts never run out. So remembering isn't for His sake. It's for ours.
The remembering is the lunch. Forget it, and by four o'clock the whole soul is running on empty.

how: Aakhaa jeevaa is the third shabad of Rehras Sahib, recited each evening; remembering the Name, simran, through the day is central to Sikh practice, and some Sikhs repeat Waheguru quietly while they work.

o: learning the hymns by heart, word for word
thinking back on the good old days
keeping the Name in mind, as food for life

games.q: the third shabad — tap the pairs.
p: my mother, as in the Anand

s: the shabad says chanting the Name is easy
it says it's hard to keep saying the True Name.
the shabad says the Lord would grow greater if everyone praised Him
He wouldn't grow greater, or less; remembering is for our sake.
the refrain asks: how could I forget Him, my mother?

games.q: Guru Nanak talks about hunger in this shabad. what does the right hunger do?
o: hunger for the Name eats up pain.
it should be cured by fasting.
games.why: usually hunger is the problem; here, hunger for the True Name is the cure, consuming sorrow.

practice: Let the day's noise settle, then gently remember: if you pray, say Waheguru once, slowly, and let it be the meal you skipped; if you don't, hold the one thing that keeps you going, a person, a purpose, a quiet you trust.
When the mind wanders back into the day, that's forgetting; notice it, and remember again.

wordCard.voice: Remembering. Aakhaa jeevaa visrai mar jaao: saying the Name, I live; forgetting it, I die. The third shabad of Rehras, by Guru Nanak.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: aakhaa jeevaa, saying it, I live; the opening of the third shabad of Rehras.

carryVoice: Your line: remember and live. The remembering is for us, not for Him. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Asa M1, aakhaa jeevaa visrai mar jaao, Ang 9
